passages.t: The rich man and the poor man in the meeting
passages.happening:
“My brothers, as you hold out your faith in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ, do not show favoritism” (verse 1).

Then James paints a scene. “Suppose a man comes into your meeting wearing a gold ring and fine clothes, and a poor man in shabby clothes also comes in. If you lavish attention on the man in fine clothes and say, ‘Here is a seat of honor,’ but say to the poor man, ‘You must stand’ or ‘Sit at my feet,’ have you not discriminated among yourselves and become judges with evil thoughts?” (verses 2-4).

“Listen, my beloved brothers: Has not God chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith and to inherit the kingdom He promised those who love Him? But you have dishonored the poor. Is it not the rich who oppress you and drag you into court? Are they not the ones who blaspheme the noble name by which you have been called?” (verses 5-7).
passages.hearers:
‘Favoritism’ translates a Greek word that means, literally, ‘receiving the face’: judging by who a person is rather than by what they have done. James sets it beside ‘our glorious Lord Jesus Christ’. If you believe in the Lord of glory, why would a gold ring dazzle you?

In the ancient world, clothes and jewellery announced a person's rank. A gold ring could mark a man of the upper class. At banquets, at the theatre and in public gatherings, people were seated by rank, and the powerful expected honour. So what James describes is simply how every other gathering in the city worked. That is why it was so tempting to let it happen in church too.

The word for ‘meeting’ is synagōgē, the word for a synagogue. The first Jewish believers in Jesus could call their gathering by that name. It is one sign that the letter comes from a very early, Jewish-Christian setting.

Then James asks three sharp questions. Has God not chosen the poor? Many of these believers were poor labourers or tenants, and God had made them ‘rich in faith’ and heirs of his kingdom. And who was hurting them? The rich, who dragged them into court, probably over debts or wages, and who spoke against the name of Christ. Some of these rich were most likely outsiders, hostile to the faith. Yet the church was bowing to them.

James does not say that God loves the poor and hates the rich. He says that God has set his love on people the world overlooks, and that a church which copies the world's seating plan has forgotten whose house it is.
passages.ot:
The law forbade favouritism in judging: “You must not pervert justice; you must not show partiality to the poor or favoritism to the rich; you are to judge your neighbor fairly” (Leviticus 19:15).

The wisdom books teach that rich and poor stand alike before God: “The rich and the poor have this in common: The LORD is Maker of them all” (Proverbs 22:2). And, “Whoever oppresses the poor taunts their Maker, but whoever is kind to the needy honors Him” (Proverbs 14:31).

When Samuel was looking for a king among Jesse's sons, God told him, “For man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7).
passages.asks: Picture the person who would be least welcome in your church, or in your home. Ask how you would greet them. Ask where you give better seats, real or pictured, to the wealthy, the attractive or the useful. And ask whom God might be lifting up that you have overlooked.

passages.t: The royal law, and mercy over judgment
passages.happening:
“If you really fulfill the royal law stated in Scripture, ‘Love your neighbor as yourself,’ you are doing well. But if you show favoritism, you sin and are convicted by the law as transgressors” (verses 8-9).

“Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles at just one point is guilty of breaking all of it. For He who said, ‘Do not commit adultery,’ also said, ‘Do not murder.’ If you do not commit adultery, but do commit murder, you have become a lawbreaker” (verses 10-11).

“Speak and act as those who are going to be judged by the law that gives freedom. For judgment without mercy will be shown to anyone who has not been merciful. Mercy triumphs over judgment” (verses 12-13).
passages.hearers:
James answers favouritism with the law itself. Love for your neighbour is ‘the royal law’, the law of the King. Jesus himself named it the second great commandment. Love does not pick and choose by rank.

Then James makes a point about the law as a whole. The law is not a pile of separate rules, where you can keep most and break a few. It is the word of one God. Break any part and you have broken faith with the one who spoke all of it. So the person who would never commit adultery, but treats the poor with contempt, is still a lawbreaker. Favouritism is not a small thing.

‘The law that gives freedom’ is the same phrase James used in 1:25. He means God's law as Jesus taught and fulfilled it: the law of love, which sets people free.

And then the great line: ‘Mercy triumphs over judgment.’ Those who refuse mercy to others will meet judgment without mercy. But mercy, given and received, wins over judgment. This is the same as Jesus' word, ‘Blessed are the merciful’.
passages.ot:
James quotes the law of Leviticus: “love your neighbor as yourself. I am the LORD” (Leviticus 19:18). Jesus called it the second commandment: “The second is this: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’ No other commandment is greater than these” (Mark 12:31).

The two commands he names come from the Ten Commandments: “You shall not murder. You shall not commit adultery” (Exodus 20:13-14).

And the prophets put mercy at the heart of what God wants: “For I desire mercy, not sacrifice” (Hosea 6:6). “And what does the LORD require of you but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?” (Micah 6:8).
passages.hard:
‘Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles at just one point is guilty of breaking all of it.’ Does this mean that every sin is equally bad?

Not quite. James's point is about the law's unity, not about the size of each sin. The law is one because the Lawgiver is one, so any breaking of it is a breaking of faith with him. James uses this against people who thought favouritism did not count because they kept the bigger commands.

The Bible does treat some wrongs as weightier than others. Jesus spoke of ‘the weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy, and faithfulness’ (Matthew 23:23). Some sins do more harm to others and call for more serious answers. But no one can stand before God on a record of keeping most of the law. That is why James ends with mercy: all of us need it, and all of us are called to give it.
passages.asks: Ask whether there is a part of God's law you treat as small because you keep the bigger parts. Ask whom you have judged without mercy. And ask what it would mean to speak and act today as someone who will be judged by the law of love.

passages.happening:
“What good is it, my brothers, if someone claims to have faith, but has no deeds? Can such faith save him? Suppose a brother or sister is without clothes and daily food. If one of you tells him, ‘Go in peace; stay warm and well fed,’ but does not provide for his physical needs, what good is that? So too, faith by itself, if it does not result in action, is dead” (verses 14-17).

“But someone will say, ‘You have faith and I have deeds.’ Show me your faith without deeds, and I will show you my faith by my deeds. You believe that God is one. Good for you! Even the demons believe that—and shudder. O foolish man, do you want evidence that faith without deeds is worthless?” (verses 18-20).

“Was not our father Abraham justified by what he did when he offered his son Isaac on the altar? You see that his faith was working with his actions, and his faith was perfected by what he did. And the Scripture was fulfilled that says, ‘Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness,’ and he was called a friend of God. As you can see, a man is justified by his deeds and not by faith alone” (verses 21-24).

“In the same way, was not even Rahab the prostitute justified by her actions when she welcomed the spies and sent them off on another route? As the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without deeds is dead” (verses 25-26).
passages.hearers:
Notice the word ‘claims’ in verse 14. James is speaking about someone who says he has faith. The question is whether that kind of faith, a faith of words only, can save.

His first picture is painfully simple. A believer is cold and hungry. Another believer says, ‘Go in peace’, adds a cheerful wish, and walks away. Words without help are useless to the hungry. So is faith without deeds.

Then James answers an imagined objector, in the style of Greek moral teaching, with a pretend debating partner. The objector says that some people have faith and others have deeds, as if they were two separate gifts. James says no. Faith shows itself by what it does. You cannot see faith that does nothing.

‘You believe that God is one.’ That is the Shema, the confession every devout Jew said each day. Good, says James, but the demons believe it too, and tremble. Agreeing that something is true is not the same as trusting God. The faith James attacks is a creed held without trust or obedience.

‘Worthless’ in verse 20 is, in Greek, argē, from a word that means ‘without work’. It is a play on words: faith without works does no work. Some manuscripts read ‘dead’ here instead, as in verses 17 and 26; the BSB follows those that read ‘worthless’.

Then two examples, chosen on purpose to be as different as possible. Abraham was the honoured father of Israel. Rahab was a Canaanite woman and a prostitute in Jericho. Yet both showed their faith by what they did. Abraham trusted God enough to obey the hardest command of his life. Rahab trusted Israel's God enough to hide his people's spies at the risk of her own life. Long before that test, God had counted Abraham's faith as righteousness (Genesis 15). Decades later, on the mountain, that faith was shown to be real and was ‘perfected’, brought to its goal.

Last, a picture everyone understood. A body without breath is a corpse. Faith without deeds is a corpse too.
passages.ot:
James quotes Genesis: “Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness” (Genesis 15:6). Years later, after Abraham had offered Isaac, the angel said, “for now I know that you fear God, since you have not withheld your only son from me” (Genesis 22:12).

‘A friend of God’ is what the Old Testament calls him: “the descendants of Abraham Your friend” (2 Chronicles 20:7); “descendant of Abraham My friend” (Isaiah 41:8).

Rahab's story is in Joshua. “But the woman had taken the two men and hidden them” (Joshua 2:4), and she let them down by a rope from her window in the city wall. She confessed, “for the LORD your God is God in the heavens above and on the earth below” (Joshua 2:11). Joshua spared her and her family, “So she has lived among the Israelites to this day” (Joshua 6:25).

And the prophets had long said what living faith does: “Isn’t it to share your bread with the hungry, to bring the poor and homeless into your home, to clothe the naked when you see him” (Isaiah 58:7).
passages.hard:
James says “a man is justified by his deeds and not by faith alone” (verse 24). Paul says “a man is justified by faith apart from works of the law” (Romans 3:28). How can both be true?

Start with what all the churches confess. Salvation is God's gift, by his grace. No one earns it, and no one can boast. And the faith that saves is never dead: Paul himself says, “All that matters is faith, expressed through love” (Galatians 5:6).

Most readers, across the churches, think James and Paul answer different questions. Paul uses ‘justify’ most often for God's verdict on a sinner; James may mean being shown to be righteous, as Abraham's faith was shown on the mountain. Paul means by ‘faith’ trust in Christ; James attacks bare agreement, the kind demons have. Paul rejects works of the law as the ground of acceptance; James asks for deeds of mercy as faith's fruit. Some think James was answering people who had twisted Paul's teaching into an excuse.

The churches still put verse 24 differently. Protestant churches teach that a person is justified by faith alone, as God's verdict, and that good works always follow as its fruit and evidence; many read verse 24 as faith shown to be real. The Catholic Church teaches that grace comes first and is never earned, and that by grace a person is truly made righteous; the Council of Trent in 1547 read verse 24 as growth in justification through good works done by God's grace. The Orthodox churches speak of salvation as union with God and the healing of the whole person, and justification never became a dividing question for them. In 1999 Catholics and Lutherans signed a joint statement that we are accepted by God by grace alone, through faith in Christ's saving work, not by any merit of ours, while naming differences that remain.

These notes do not choose. The book page and the doctrine study ‘Justification’ set out each view more fully.
passages.asks: Think of someone you know who is cold, hungry or alone. Ask whether your faith has done anything for them, or only wished them well. Ask whether your faith is trust in God, or only agreement with the right words. And ask what it would look like this week for your faith to work with your actions.
